FUNCTIONS

Usually have this form  

```{r}

# don't run these
X <- function(object, argument1, argument2, argument3)

```


PLOT

```{r}

#create some datasets, first a vector of 1-100 and 101-200
# c means combine

Data1 <- c(1:100)
Data2 <- c(101:200)

#Plot the data
plot(Data1, Data2, col="red")

```


```{r}
#just for fun, create some more, this time some normally distributed
#vectors of 100 numbers

Data3 <- rnorm(100, mean = 53, sd=34)
Data4 <- rnorm(100, mean = 64, sd=14)

#plot
plot(Data3, Data4, col="blue")

```

TO GET HELP try

```{r}
?plot

```

DATA STRUCTURES

These include 

[must only contain data of the same type (e.g. numeric or text)]
a matrix, 
an array, 
a vector, 

[mixture of data types (e.g. numeric and text)]
a data frame and 
a list.

```{r}
# define a dataframe

df <- data.frame(Data1, Data2)
plot(df, col="green")

```

```{r}
#see only a selection of a large dataframe

library(tidyverse)

#show the first 10 and then last 10 rows of data in df...
df %>%
  head()
```

```{r}
df %>%
  tail()
```

%>% is a pipe  "THEN" [from 'magrittr' package]
|> is also a pipe 

to get to ELEMENTS ON THE DATAFRAME

```{r}
# Don't run
# use the single square bracket [] operator
# to select, or subset

data.frame[row,column]
```

```{r}
df[1:10, 1]
df[5:15,]
df[c(2,3,6),2]
df[,1]

```

```{r}
library(dplyr)

df <- df %>%
  dplyr::rename(column1 = Data1, column2=Data2)

```

```{r}
df %>% 
  dplyr::select(column2)
```

TO CALL COLUMNS BY THEIR NAME
(A) use dplyr (see above) or
(B) use '$' operator or
(C) use double square bracket '[[]]' operator, and refer to our column by name using quotes 

```{r}

# Do not run
# The form to call for an specific column in dataframe is

data.frame$columnName

# now aplying it

df$column1

df[['column2']]
```

OLD SKOOL CLEANING

```{r}
?read.csv2

#check what separator the file uses

readLines("Prac2_data/LondonData.csv", n = 5)

#it shows semicolon ";"

LondonDataOSK <- read.table("Prac2_data/LondonData.csv", 
                         header = TRUE,
                         sep = ";",
                         fileEncoding = "Windows-1252"
                         )
```


NOW, BRING THE DATA STRAIGHT FROM THE WEBSITE

```{r}
#wang the data in straight from the web using read_csv, 
#skipping over the 'n/a' entries as you go...

LondonData <- read_csv("https://data.london.gov.uk/download/f33fb38c-cb37-48e3-8298-84c0d3cc5a6c/772d2d64-e8c6-46cb-86f9-e52b4c7851bc/ward-profiles-excel-version.csv",
                       locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"),
                       na = "n/a")

```

```{r}
# Check the new data

class(LondonData)
```

```{r}
# or, if you have your old skool data
class(LondonDataOSK)
```

```{r}
Datatypelist <- LondonData %>% 
  summarise_all(class) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to="All_variables", 
               values_to="Variable_class")

Datatypelist
```


```{r}
summary(df)
```

```{r}
LondonData%>%
  colnames()%>%
  # just look at the head, top5
  head()
```

SELECT SOME ROWS

```{r}
LondonBoroughs<-LondonData[626:658,]

# or with dplyr

LondonBoroughs<-LondonData%>%
  dplyr::slice(626:658)
```

OTHER COOL WAY IS FILTER

```{r}
Femalelifeexp<- LondonData %>% 
  filter(`Female life expectancy -2009-13`>90)

```

OR DETECT -USE WITH STRINGS-

```{r}
library(stringr)

LondonBoroughs<- LondonData %>% 
  filter(str_detect(`New code`, "^E09"))

LondonBoroughs$`Ward name`
```

```{r}
LondonBoroughs %>% 
  dplyr::select(`Ward name`) %>%
  print()
```
```{r}

#  you will have two rows at the top for the City of London
# get unique values

LondonBoroughs<-LondonBoroughs %>%
  distinct()
```

SELECT COLUMNS

```{r}
#select columns 1,19,20 and 21
LondonBoroughs_manualcols<-LondonBoroughs[,c(1,19,20,21)]

# or you can also

LondonBoroughs_dplyrcols<-LondonBoroughs %>%
  dplyr::select(c(1,19,20,21))

```

COOL WAY

```{r}

LondonBoroughs_contains<-LondonBoroughs %>% 
  dplyr::select(contains("expectancy"), 
         contains("obese - 2011/12 to 2013/14"),
         contains("Ward name")) 
```
